nature-econ-641.title: Transaction costs: the price of making a deal
nature-econ-641.text: Every trade costs more than its price. A transaction cost is any cost of making a trade in a market, over and above the price of the thing traded. Economists sort these costs into three groups: search and information costs, bargaining and decision costs, and policing and enforcement costs. John R. Commons introduced the idea in 1931 that transactions are the basis of economic thinking. The term is often wrongly credited to Coase, though his 1937 paper The Nature of the Firm did discuss the 'costs of using the price mechanism'. Douglass North argued that a society's rules, its institutions, largely set transaction costs, and that institutions keeping them low can help an economy grow. The costs bite in environmental markets too. High transaction costs, such as proving that a project would not have happened anyway, have long troubled carbon offset schemes like {{ref:nature-mkt-104}}.

nature-econ-632.title: Excludability: can non-payers be kept out
nature-econ-632.text: A cinema can check tickets at the door. A lighthouse cannot stop a passing ship from using its light. That difference is excludability: how far the supplier of a good can stop people who have not paid from using it. Economists describe every good by two traits, how excludable it is and how rival it is. Paul Samuelson proposed the idea in 1954 as a yes-or-no trait. Ostrom recast it in 1990 as a scale, from fully excludable to fully non-excludable. Music, films and software sit in between: they have a price, but piracy lets many non-payers use them. The trait matters because producers cannot profit from goods people get free. Without government help, non-excludable goods therefore tend to be under-supplied.

nature-econ-625.title: Rivalry: does my use leave less for you
nature-econ-625.text: Once someone eats an apple, no one else can. A TV broadcast is different: one more viewer takes nothing from the rest. A good is rival when one person's use of it stops or reduces others' use at the same time. It is non-rival when serving one more person costs nothing extra, as with a scenic view, clean air or street lights. Non-rival does not mean cheap. The total cost of providing the good can be large; only the cost of one more user is zero. Many goods are non-rival only up to a point. Roads, the internet and courts slow everyone down once congestion sets in, so economists now treat rivalry as a scale rather than a yes-or-no. Paul Samuelson introduced non-rival consumption in 1954 to separate goods shared by all, {{ref:nature-econ-633}}, from ordinary goods. Richard Musgrave later added rivalry and excludability as criteria.

nature-econ-633.title: Public goods: shared by all, paid for by few
nature-econ-633.text: No one can be kept from the safety a flood control system provides, and one more protected house takes nothing from the next. That makes it a public good: a good or service that no one can be kept from using and that one person's use does not reduce for others. Knowledge, official statistics, national security, aids to navigation and street lighting are other examples. So are clean air and many other goods from the environment. Public goods are usually supplied by government and paid for by taxes, for a simple reason. People who do not pay can still use them, so public goods may be under-produced, overused or degraded, the trouble explored in {{ref:nature-econ-617}}. Private firms find them unprofitable, so without government they might be produced only in small amounts or not at all. Paul Samuelson set out the modern theory in his 1954 paper The Pure Theory of Public Expenditure, building on Wicksell and Lindahl. Yet public goods need not come from the public sector. They can occur naturally, or be produced by individuals, firms or community groups. Technology can change a good's status: encryption lets broadcasters sell access, and cheaper ways of charging for roads allow drivers to pay by actual use. Pure public goods are rare. Economists still debate how to define them, whether they form a real category at all, and how serious the problems they cause are.

nature-econ-610.title: Common-pool resources: hard to fence, easy to deplete
nature-econ-610.text: A fishing ground is hard to fence, yet every fish one boat takes is a fish another cannot. That combination defines a common-pool resource. It is a natural or human-made resource system, such as fishing grounds or an irrigation system, that is costly but not impossible to keep people from using. Forests, groundwater basins, pastures and the atmosphere are other examples. Unlike pure public goods, these resources get crowded or overused, because what one user takes is no longer there for others. Without management the logic is grim. Each fisher has a reason to catch as many fish as possible before someone else does, so fish stocks soon run down. Ownership varies. Governments may hold such resources as public goods, communities as common property, and individuals or firms as private holdings. When no one owns them, they are open access. A common claim held that such resources must be privatized or be destroyed. Ostrom found many run by local self-managing communities, contradicting that claim. In James Bay, Quebec, beaver numbers recovered after Indigenous communities' customary hunting laws were legally recognized and outside trappers were banned.

nature-econ-606.title: The tragedy of the commons: when shared means overused
nature-econ-606.text: In 1833 the English economist Lloyd described herders sharing a common pasture. Each could add extra cattle, and together the extra cattle could lead to overgrazing. The tragedy of the commons is the idea behind that scene. When people share a resource that benefits each user at a cost to everyone, each has a reason to overuse it, so together they use it up. The name comes from a 1968 essay in the journal Science by the ecologist Hardin, who took his title from Lloyd's pamphlet. Hardin's main worry was that there would be too many people, and he wrote that 'freedom in a commons brings ruin to all'. The idea now serves as a model for many resource problems, including water, forests, fish, and oil, gas and coal. Climate change has been described as a huge example, with the Earth treated as a commons depleted without regard to the harm done to others. Proposed government fixes include privatization, regulation such as permits for fishing or logging, and making users pay for the harm they cause. Whether the tragedy is inevitable is disputed. Ostrom and colleagues found it less common and easier to solve than Hardin claimed, because local users often design their own rules. Farmers have run one Swiss Alpine commons since 1517. Critics add that historical English common land always had a legal owner, and only people with legal rights, called commoners, could use it.

nature-econ-617.title: The free-rider problem: benefiting without paying
nature-econ-617.text: A coastal town's lighthouse guides ships from many countries, and those ships pay nothing toward it. That is the free-rider problem: a market failure that happens when people who benefit from a shared resource or public good pay nothing, or too little, for it. Because no one can be kept from using a public good, each person has little reason to help pay. The result is too little of the good produced, or too much of it used up, which is wasteful for society. People also hide their interest. Asked how much they would pay for a public good, they tend to understate how much they value it. The logic resembles {{ref:nature-econ-039}}. If two people should share the cost of a fire station and both refuse to pay, society gets nothing. People tend to cooperate by nature, yet the presence of free riders has been shown to make cooperation break down. Climate change is often framed this way. Every country gains from others cutting emissions, but each would lose by moving its own economy away from carbon. One way around the problem is low-cost pooling of contributions, as in internet crowdfunding, where no money changes hands until a goal is met.

nature-econ-657.title: Private goods: yours to keep, and gone once used
nature-econ-657.text: A loaf of bread is the model of a private good. Once one person eats it no one else can, and a baker can refuse to sell it. A private good is a useful good that its owner can keep others from using and that one person's use uses up for others. Private goods are scarce, which can create competition for them. Unlike public goods such as clean air, they rarely suffer from free riding. Their market demand is found by adding up how much each person will buy at each price, a method called horizontal summation. Public goods, enjoyed by everyone at once, have their individual demands summed vertically instead.

nature-econ-661.title: Public economics: when should government step in
nature-econ-661.text: When should government step into markets, and how far? Public economics studies government policy in terms of efficiency and fairness to answer that question. It builds on welfare economics and aims to improve social welfare. Its focus is market failures, such as public goods, externalities and imperfect competition, along with taxes and government spending. Examples of government action include providing defense, regulating pollution and dealing with unequal information between buyers and sellers. The field holds two classic answers to pollution. A.C. Pigou proposed taxes to correct externalities, such as a tax on emissions. In 1960 Coase proposed instead assigning ownership rights and letting people negotiate. Much of the method explored in {{ref:nature-val-001}} was developed in the United States from the problems of water-resource projects.

nature-econ-616.title: Four types of goods: a grid for every good
nature-econ-616.text: Two questions sort every good in the economy. Can people be kept from using it? And does one person's use leave less for others? The answers give a grid of four types. Goods that can be withheld and are used up are private goods, such as food, clothing and parking spaces. Goods that cannot be withheld but are used up are common-pool resources, such as fish stocks and timber. Goods that can be withheld but are not used up are the kind explored in {{ref:nature-econ-627}}, such as cinemas, software and private parks. Goods that cannot be withheld and are not used up are public goods, such as free-to-air television, air and national defense. The grid shows where trouble lies. Common-pool resources invite overuse because no one can be kept out, and public goods invite free riding for the same reason. Private goods rarely face either problem.

nature-econ-627.title: Club goods: members only, but no one else loses
nature-econ-627.text: A gym can shut out non-members, yet one more member on a quiet morning takes nothing from the others. That is a club good. People can be kept from using it, usually by charging them, but one person's use does not reduce it for others until it gets crowded. Cinemas, cable television, software as a service, and golf club or swimming pool memberships are other examples. Serving one more user costs almost nothing, so club goods are often supplied by natural monopolies and kept artificially scarce. Providers exclude non-payers either to cover fixed costs, as nonprofits do, or to make a profit. Controlling access nearly always causes a deadweight loss, such as the cost of tollbooths or digital rights management. Even the European Union has been treated as a club good. Its services can be withheld from non-members, while adding members to the Schengen Area does not make travel harder for existing ones.

nature-econ-659.title: Property: rights over things, and the things themselves
nature-econ-659.text: Property means two things at once: a system of rights giving people legal control over valuable things, and the valuable things themselves. Depending on the thing, an owner may use, change, share, rent, sell, give away or destroy it, and keep others from doing so. Economics recognizes four broad forms: private, public, collective and common. Legal systems separate land and buildings, real property, from movable personal property. One view holds that things become property only when scarce: hunter-gatherers did not treat land as property, because there was no shortage of it. Aristotle favored private ownership, arguing that self-interest leads people to neglect the commons.

nature-econ-621.title: Property rights: the rules of who owns what
nature-econ-621.text: Can anyone own the air? Some climate policies work by setting up property rights for the atmosphere. Property rights are the rules that decide who owns a resource or good and how it may be used. Resources can be owned by individuals, associations, collectives or governments. The rights come in three parts. There is the right to use a good, the right to earn income from it, and the right to sell, change, abandon or destroy it. Well-enforced rights give people reasons to invest, innovate and trade, which makes markets work better. Secure rights also make resources harder to exploit, so people are less likely to use them unsustainably. Governments can create property rights directly, through rules such as limits on discharges, or through market tools such as taxes and tradable permits. A scheme that trades permits to emit, explored in {{ref:nature-pol-253}}, creates exactly such rights over the atmosphere. The stakes are large. Studying former European colonies, Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson found strong evidence that institutions giving secure property rights lead to prosperity.

nature-econ-652.title: Land tenure: who may use land, and on what terms
nature-econ-652.text: Who may farm a field, for how long, and on what terms? Land tenure is the system that decides. It can rest on official laws and policies or on informal local customs, and it sets out the holder's rights and responsibilities toward the land. Its forms range widely. Fee simple, the most complete ownership in common law, sits alongside leasehold, life estates, shared rights to common land, sharecropping and easements. Tradeable individual ownership of land was often introduced through colonialism. Tenure matters for nature too. Land tenure and forest governance were named among the issues that national forest strategies under {{ref:nature-mkt-092}} must address.

nature-econ-658.title: Private property: ownership outside the state
nature-econ-658.text: Private property is the foundation of capitalism, and one of its most contested ideas. It means ownership by people or organizations other than the government, as distinct from public property owned by the state and from collective or cooperative property. It is a legal idea, defined and enforced by each country's legal and political institutions. John Locke's chief argument for owning land privately was that it led to better land management and farming than common land. Supporters say private ownership puts land to productive use, protects its value, and lets it be traded or used as collateral. Owners' rights usually come with limits, such as building codes or bans on demolishing historic buildings. Economic liberals see private property as essential to prosperity. Socialists criticize private ownership of the means of production, and other critics call property law a tool of empire that ignored Indigenous communities' shared holding of land.

nature-econ-649.title: Georgism: keep what you make, share what nature gives
nature-econ-649.text: Keep what you make, but share what nature provides. That is the heart of Georgism: people should own what they produce, while the income from land and natural resources should belong equally to everyone. It grew from the writings of the American economist Henry George. His first book, Progress and Poverty (1879), argued for raising public money mainly from land and natural resources. In economics, 'land' means everything in nature that exists without human effort. George included climate, soil, waterways, minerals, forests, oceans, air and solar energy. He blamed private capture of land rent for persistent poverty despite technological progress, and for boom-and-bust cycles. The main policy is a tax on land values, explored in {{ref:nature-res-143}}, whose revenue could cut or replace taxes on income, trade and purchases. Milton Friedman called a tax on unimproved land value the 'least bad tax', because it does not hold back economic activity the way other taxes do. Some Georgists want surplus revenue returned to people as a basic income or citizen's dividend.

nature-econ-612.title: Common property regimes: communities that manage their own commons
nature-econ-612.text: To outsiders a community-run resource looks private; to its members it is common. That double face marks a common property regime: a social arrangement by which a community regulates how a shared resource is kept up, maintained and used. Such systems arise when users acting alone threaten the resource's total benefit. They protect the central resource while sharing out what can be harvested, usually working locally to prevent overuse. Members have monitored access, and outsiders can be kept out. The rules must limit the amount, timing and technology of harvesting. Limits set too high destroy the resource; limits set too low waste its benefits. Such a regime is not the same as a common-pool resource, which is not always governed as common property. Nor is it open access, where entry is free. Hardin's tragedy of the commons was criticized for blurring that line. Members' local knowledge often lets these regimes outperform rules designed by outside experts, and results are best when they also consult governments and experts.

nature-econ-609.title: Solutions to the tragedy of the commons: from owners to communities
nature-econ-609.text: Finding solutions to the tragedy of the commons counts among the main problems of political philosophy. The proposals run from local, self-organized rules to government action. One is privatization. Turning a common resource into private property gives the new owner a reason to keep it productive, an idea linked to Coase in 1960. It works when the owner pays the full price of using up the resource. Another is a government cap on how much any one person may use, through permits for mining, fishing, hunting, grazing and logging. Governments step in when a community is too large for its social ties to hold it together. A middle way shares ownership between government and community, so that no one or two parties hold all the power. Cooperation can also come from below. Political scientist Robert Axelrod argues that even self-interested people often find ways to cooperate, because restraint serves both them and the group.

nature-econ-615.title: Open access resources: first come, first served
nature-econ-615.text: In an open fishery, profits draw in more fishers. More fishers leave fewer fish, scarcer fish fetch higher prices, and higher prices draw in still more fishers. That spiral is the danger of an open access resource: one that no one owns and anyone can use, where what one person takes leaves less for others. Such resources need little oversight or are hard to restrict. Because they are first come, first served, they are prone to the tragedy of the commons. The distinction from managed commons matters. Hardin's work has been criticized for failing to tell common-pool resources apart from open access resources.

nature-econ-613.title: Ostrom's design principles: what long-lived commons share
nature-econ-613.text: Ostrom did not just argue that communities could manage shared resources; she showed how. In her 1990 book, {{ref:nature-res-197}}, she reported that communities around the world had managed shared resources successfully through local governance. From the long-lasting cases she drew eight conditions. The first are clearly defined boundaries, and rules for taking and supplying the resource that fit local conditions. Most users should take part in making the rules. Monitors should be users themselves or answer to them. Rule-breakers face sanctions that grow step by step, and conflicts can be settled cheaply and easily. Authorities such as the government must at least recognize the users' right to organize. Large resources are run as layers of nested groups, with small local ones at the base. Together the principles describe arrangements in which the users themselves make, watch and enforce the rules.

nature-econ-622.title: Types of property regimes: four ways to hold a resource
nature-econ-622.text: Who controls a resource shapes how it is used. Resources can be held in four main ways, sorted by whether others can be kept out and whether use leaves less for others. Open-access property is owned by nobody and managed by nobody, and access is not controlled; an unregulated forest is an example. It can exist because ownership was never set up in law, or because keeping people out costs more than it is worth. Public or state property is owned by the public, with access and use controlled by a government agency. Private property is controlled by its owner or owners. A cellphone is an example, because only one person can use it and it must be bought. Common or collective property, in the legal sense, is owned by a group whose members jointly control access, use and exclusion.

nature-econ-643.title: Bargaining: haggling over the terms of a deal
nature-econ-643.text: Haggling has largely vanished where fixed-price shops dominate, but it survives for expensive goods such as homes, cars and jewelry. Bargaining is a kind of negotiation in which a buyer and a seller argue over the price or terms of a deal. If they agree, the trade goes ahead. Emotions, mental biases and a sense of fairness strongly affect it. One bias, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-033}}, makes sellers ask more than buyers will pay. Coase argued that without transaction costs, people would bargain their way to the same use of resources however a court ruled in a property dispute.

openers.public-goods-commons-and-property: Some goods can be fenced off and get used up; others can be kept from no one and leave just as much for the next user. Economists sort every good by those two questions: whether people can be kept from using it, and whether one person's use leaves less for others. The answers explain why goods open to all are usually supplied by government and paid for by taxes, why people who benefit from shared resources tend to pay too little, and why resources such as fishing grounds and irrigation systems get used up. This chapter follows those problems and the remedies people have tried, from public provision to systems of property rights, along with the costs of making a trade that shape them all.
